newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICAN PARAFFIN PRICE HIKES HIT POOR HARD.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICAN PARAFFIN PRICE HIKES HIT POOR HARD.

text.p: A weak rand and high oil prices have proved a double blow for South African motorists -- but millions of poor households are equally hard hit even though they do not own a car.
These households use paraffin as their main sources of cooking, heating and lighting.
Paraffin use has more than doubled to eight billion litres in the last 10 years, although it should now start to fall as an ambitious programme of household electrification takes root.
In the meantime, according to the Poverty Profile newsletter produced by Idasa, paraffin accounts for between four and 12 percent of the monthly spending of poor households.
"Increases in the prices of paraffin have a direct impact on the women who manage the households as they usually look after the energy needs," it said.

The inland wholesale price of a litre of paraffin has risen to 136.43 cents from 122.43 cents in February. Retailers are allowed a 33.3 percent mark-up but this is difficult to regulate and mark-ups of more than 100 percent are not unheard of.

This is especially the case in the "spaza" or informal shops in the townships which usually decant paraffin from large containers into cold drink bottles for easier sale in small quantities to the poor.
Poverty Profile said a new women's group, Women's Movement, had launched a campaign to help reduce the cost of paraffin by removing VAT presently levied on it by government.
"Compared to other goods, removing VAT on paraffin would be an exceptionally well targeted form of assistance to the poorest of the poor," Poverty Profile said.
"Other zero-rated goods are consumed by both the poor and the non-poor. But in the case of paraffin, this would not be the case because very few higher income households use it."
